Abstract

emphasizes but that a converged teacher attenuates are precisely the shortcut directions
worth pushing the student away from. We instantiate this observation as Anti-Shortcut
Distillation (ASD), a push–pull KD framework that treats the converged teacher

Introduction
<sub>2</sub>Knowledge distillation (KD) [11, 16] compresses a high-capacity teacher into a compact stu-
:dent by transferring supervisory structure richer than one-hot labels. Recent methods have
expanded the types of knowledge transferred during distillation: FitNets [27] regresses in-
Xtermediate features, AT [35] matches spatial attention, RKD [24] and PKT [25] preserve
rsample geometry, CRD [30] adds contrastive transfer, DKD [37] decouples logits, and Re-
<sup>a</sup>viewKD [3] aggregates feature hierarchies, but all share one geometric premise: distillation
is treated as a unilateral attractive force. The student is pulled toward the teacher, but the ob-
jective is silent about which representational directions the student should avoid. Repulsive
sample-level negatives [30], checkpoint-based positive targets [32], and bias-aware distilla-
tion [20, 22] partially address this asymmetry, but none uses the teacher itself to identify
harmful representational directions.

This asymmetry matters because teacher representations are themselves products of a
temporal optimization path. Networks tend to exploit local textures, colour statistics, and
background cues early in training before consolidating shape-biased, semantically stable
features [1, 9, 10]. A converged teacher records the endpoint of this process, not the shortcut-
prone directions traversed and attenuated along the way. A compact student trained under
the same data distribution may therefore recover the easiest spurious correlations available,
weakening robustness under corruption and shift [13, 28, 29]. The teacher’s trajectory thus
carries a second form of knowledge: not only features worth imitating, but also directions
worth rejecting.
We introduce Anti-Shortcut Distillation (ASD) to convert this latent trajectory signal into
explicit push–pull supervision (fig. 1). ASD treats the converged teacher

This sharply separates ASD from prior trajectory-aware distillation [8, 17, 23, 32, 36]: inter-

directions from which the student should be separated.

contrastive loss

Lukasik et al. [22] show distillation amplifies teacher errors on subgroups; Lee & Lee [20]
debias by transplanting the teacher’s last layer. Both diagnose when transfer is harmful at
the label/head level; ASD operationalizes the harmful directions, extracting them label-free
from the early-to-final displacement. Networks fit simple, dominant patterns before more ro-
bust structure [1, 29]; in image classification this manifests as texture bias [9, 10], weakening
robustness under shift [13, 28]. ASD targets this failure mode at distillation time using the
teacher’s own early-to-final feature change as a label-free shortcut indicator. SimCLR [4],
MoCo [12], and memory-bank methods [33] learn invariances by separating positives from
negatives; supervised contrastive learning [18] adds label structure; CRD [30] brings con-

positives and negatives are distinct optimization states of the same teacher.

trainable student, the frozen converged teacher, and a frozen early teacher checkpoint. The
final teacher provides the semantic target to imitate, whereas the early teacher exposes
shortcut-biased directions that should not be transferred to the student. This section de-
scribes how ASD converts this teacher trajectory into two coupled mechanisms: temporal
contrastive alignment (section 3.3) and eigenvector-based shortcut suppression (section 3.4).
